I. Mineralogical Background: High-Iron Zijintu Clay of Mt. Fenghuang, Hangzhou
During the Northern-Southern Song transition, the Southern Song court rebuilt its Imperial Guan Kilns at Xiuneisi and Jiaotanxia in Lin'an (Hangzhou). Unlike the white high-alumina kaolin of northern Quyang Ding ware, Hangzhou abounded in hematite- and limonite-rich "Purple-Gold Clay" (Zijintu). XRF measurements show that Southern Song Guan dark gray bodies contain 3.5% to 5.2% Fe₂O₃ by weight, occasionally nearing 6%.

II. High-Temperature Fluid Mechanics & Surface Tension: Formation of the "Purple Rim"
To achieve a jade-like "thin body, thick glaze" aesthetic, Guan vessels underwent 3–4 dip and spray coats after bisque firing, reaching glaze thicknesses of 1.5–2.2 mm. At 1230°C–1260°C, the lime-alkali glaze melts into a viscous silicate liquid. Around the tight-curvature mouth rim, gravity sag and surface tension draw the molten glaze down to 0.2–0.3 mm, allowing the dark reduced body to glow faintly through translucent celadon as the understated "Purple Rim" (Zikou).

III. Re-Oxidation & Neo-Confucian Ideal: Aesthetic Elevation of the "Iron Foot"
To prevent thick glaze from fusing to kiln setters, glaze was scraped cleanly off the footrim edge. As air (O₂) re-entered the cooling kiln, scorching exposed FeO rapidly re-oxidized into magnetite (Fe₃O₄) and hematite (Fe₂O₃), yielding a rugged cast-iron dark brown known as the "Iron Foot" (Tiezu)—celebrated by Song literati as a metaphor for the gentleman: jade-gentle outside, iron-steadfast within.

I. Quantitative Model of CTE Mismatch
Let the linear thermal expansion coefficient of the ceramic body be $\alpha_b$ and that of the glaze be $\alpha_g$. In Song Ge and Guan systems, the Ca-Na-K glaze has $\alpha_g \approx 7.2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$, while high-silica Zijintu clay has $\alpha_b \approx 5.4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ K}^{-1}$. Cooling from $T_g \approx 700^{\circ}\text{C}$ to room temperature $T_0$ induces biaxial residual tensile stress in the glaze: $\sigma_g = \frac{E_g}{1 - \nu_g}(\alpha_g - \alpha_b)(T_g - T_0)$.

II. Staged Evolution of Primary (Iron-Wire) & Secondary (Gold-Thread) Crackle
Once $\sigma_g$ exceeds fracture toughness $K_{IC}$ between 220°C and 120°C, brittle cracking rings out like struck chimes, forming coarse primary fissures stained carbon-black into "Iron Wires". Over days and months afterward, atmospheric moisture drives stress corrosion on strained Si–O–Si bonds, propagating fine secondary meshes stained golden-amber by tea or iron ions into "Gold Threads".

III. Computational Graphics Simulation: Voronoi & Stress Relaxation
Our 3D gallery uses dual-layer Voronoi distance fields and first-order bump/normal mapping in WebGL shaders to reproduce orthogonal intersections of bold dark primary veins and fine golden tributaries.

I. Restraint of Hue, Elevation of Texture
While modern industrial swatches chase high saturation, Song monochrome glazes—Sky Blue, Powder Celadon, Moonlight White, Ivory—deliberately soften chroma so light dwells within translucent microcrystalline layers via subsurface scattering. As Su Shi wrote: "Reveal richness within archaic simplicity; lodge supreme flavor in tranquil plainness."

II. Cosmic Order Within a Single Curve
Stripped of ornate painting, Song porcelain distills all aesthetic tension into one continuous S-spline silhouette: the meiping stands like an upright scholar, the yuhuchun poises like a falling dewdrop, and the narcissus bowl rests calm as an autumn lake—governed by golden proportions and hydrostatic poise.

III. Mission of Digital Heritage: From Glass Cases to Living Resonance
We built the "Vessels of China · Tianqing Nihuo" platform so students and the public can use 3D inspection, fingertip wheel-throwing, and pentatonic porcelain chimes to touch eight millennia of human warmth shaped from earth and fire.
